**Title:** Which Dollar Broke? Separating Token Failures from Platform-Ledger Failures in Web Dollar Markets

**Abstract (300 words):**

In October 2018 our monitor saw Bitfinex's dollar slip below bank money 3 days before its deposit freeze was reported and 6.5 months before regulators disclosed the loss behind it. Web price feeds and oracles miss this because they average exchange prices as if all used the same dollar. CoinMarketCap dropped Bitfinex by hand only in May 2019, 7 months later. Some exchanges quote in stablecoins, others in balances on their own ledger that reach bank money only through their banks. When that link breaks, the exchange's dollar drifts, and feeds read it as a price move or stablecoin failure. Telling the failures apart is hard because an exchange's dollar is never quoted directly and any one asset may carry its own shock. Building on the law of one price and triangular arbitrage, we use bitcoin, which has no peg: its price gap between the troubled exchange and one whose banking still works measures the ledger's loss of value, and the rest of a stablecoin's dislocation belongs to the token. We accept this split only when an unrelated asset shows the same gap, the implied token price matches its direct price elsewhere, and the exchange's internal cross-rates hold. In banking cut-offs at three exchanges, 2017 to 2023, the exchange's dollar broke on Bitfinex and Binance.US but barely moved on Binance's sterling and euro rails. On Bitfinex it fell by up to 844 basis points (bps), with bitcoin and ether agreeing to within 7.2 bps. On each exchange, one episode swung from discount to premium before recovering. A multi-exchange bitcoin index was off by at least 100 bps for 2,826 hours, and dropping exchange-hours our monitor flagged removed 88% of them. In the March 2023 USD Coin run the method instead attributed the dislocation to the token. All findings are descriptive.

**Suggested keywords:** stablecoins; platform money; exchange ledgers; price feeds and oracles; Web measurement; natural experiment; reproducibility
